source.title: Blackbox meets blackbox: Representational Similarity and Stability Analysis of Neural Language Models and Brains
source.authors: Samira Abnar; Lisa Beinborn; Rochelle Choenni; Willem Zuidema

record.tranche_reason: The study compares representational similarity across language models and reports that some spaces differ substantially, refining the idea of broad convergence. It does not test whether alignment increases with scale.
record.gate_note: The study reports cross-model RSA results that bear on partial convergence (V7). It does not vary model scale or capability, compare vision and language models on paired images and captions, compare random seeds, test mappings between representations, or identify recurring features. Its ReStA context-length results compare instances of the same model, and its model-to-brain results do not measure convergence between independent models.
record.test_reason: Section 4.2 uses RSA to compare independently trained language models with different architectures and objectives. UniSentEnc is reported as very different from ELMO, GoogleLM and BERT. BERT is closer to the LSTM models, which the authors tentatively attribute to the shared language-modelling objective. This bears on V7: alignment is incomplete, and a shared objective rather than shared architecture tracks similarity. There is no scale, seed, cross-modal, mapping or feature test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that architecture and training objective both noticeably affect learned representations, and suggest the shared LM objective may explain why BERT is closer to the LSTM models than UniSentEnc is. They also conclude that LSTM models align best with brain data, though all model-brain similarities are very low. The story-reading fMRI shows shallow, not deep, linguistic processing.
record.recipe_differences: Uses RSA to compare representational similarity, but does not perform the scale sweep central to the Platonic claim; it also studies model stability as context changes and model-to-brain similarity.
record.method_sensitivity: For ReStA, the representations are compared across different context lengths. That analysis concerns within-model stability, not cross-model convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Model-to-brain RSA is low for all models (roughly 0.1-0.4, vs about 0.55 between human subjects). LSTM models align best with the brain, and NLP task performance does not correlate with brain similarity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More capable language models are not necessarily more aligned with human brain representations of the same text.

fits_no_version.finding: ReStA shows that within-model representations change with context length: LSTM first layers stabilise after about 3 sentences, while BERT keeps changing. First-to-last layer RSA is about 0.75-0.80 for the LSTMs vs about 0.35 for BERT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within-model stability of representations under input-context changes differs by architecture.

record.problems: The study uses a single story-reading dataset. The cross-model RSA comparisons are described qualitatively in the text and shown in Figure 3 without numeric values in the supplied text. It does not test scale or model capability.
record.rows_left_out: Other pairwise comparisons visible only in Figure 3 are not separately described in the text, so their individual results were not extracted.

untested.parts: No variation in model scale or capability.
Text-only models; no vision-language paired data.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation test; RSA only.
A single metric (cosine-within, Pearson-across RSA) and a single dataset; metric and input choices are not varied for cross-model comparisons.
No plateau with scale is tested. The objective explanation is a post-hoc interpretation ('could indicate'), not a controlled manipulation of training data or objective.

missing.what: Numeric pairwise cross-model RSA values (including GloVe and per-layer pairs). These appear only in the heatmaps and cannot be read from the text.

record.verdict_notes: Weak evidence for V7: one dataset, one metric, qualitative description of a heatmap, and a hedged causal attribution. The record's 'partial' states were judged against full convergence rather than against V7 itself, so they are recoded as observed for V7. Not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No vision-language model comparison on paired images and captions.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test.
No test for recurring interpretable features or circuits.
The study does not vary the similarity metric or test whether cross-model convergence depends on the input data or metric settings.

The study compares selected language-model representations on story-reading inputs, but does not test scale-related plateaus or establish that shared data or objectives cause the observed similarities.

rows.subject: UniSentEnc and ELMO

conditions.value: RSA; cosine similarity within spaces and Pearson correlation across similarity matrices

rows.measure: Representational similarity between the two models
rows.value: figure only; text describes UniSentEnc as learning very different representations from ELMO
rows.note: The paper attributes the difference as potentially related to training objectives.
rows.check: For V7 the effect is incomplete alignment explained by objective differences. Text says UniSentEnc learns 'very different representations' from ELMO, so state should be observed, not partial. Value is figure-only and unreadable from the text.

rows.subject: UniSentEnc and GoogleLM

conditions.value: RSA; cosine similarity within spaces and Pearson correlation across similarity matrices

rows.measure: Representational similarity between the two models
rows.value: figure only; text describes UniSentEnc as learning very different representations from GoogleLM
rows.note: The paper attributes the difference as potentially related to training objectives.
rows.check: Same as r1: very different spaces for UniSentEnc vs GoogleLM, consistent with V7. Figure-only value.

rows.subject: UniSentEnc and BERT (base)

conditions.value: RSA; cosine similarity within spaces and Pearson correlation across similarity matrices

rows.measure: Representational similarity between the two models
rows.value: figure only; text describes UniSentEnc as learning very different representations from BERT
rows.note: The paper notes that both are Transformer-based, while describing their spaces as very different.
rows.check: Same architecture (Transformer) but different objective yields very different spaces. This is the clearest V7-relevant contrast. Figure-only value.

rows.subject: BERT (base) and ELMO

conditions.value: RSA; cosine similarity within spaces and Pearson correlation across similarity matrices

rows.measure: Representational similarity between the two models
rows.value: figure only; text says BERT is more similar to ELMO than UniSentEnc is
rows.note: The text compares these models qualitatively and gives no numeric value for this pair.
rows.check: BERT is more similar to ELMO despite a different architecture, attributed to the shared LM objective; this matches V7's 'shared objectives explain it'. The comparison is relative only; no absolute value is given, so whether alignment is high cannot be read.

relationships.condition: Five pretrained text encoders (GloVe, ELMO, GoogleLM, BERT-base, UniSentEnc) compared with RSA on Harry Potter chapter 9 stimuli
relationships.reason: UniSentEnc differs strongly from the LM-trained models even when the architecture matches (r1-r3), while BERT is closer to the LSTM LMs (r4-r5). Similarity thus tracks the training objective rather than full convergence. Evidence is qualitative and figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: UniSentEnc differed strongly from language-model-trained encoders even with matching architecture, while BERT was closer to LSTM language models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Reported cross-model comparisons on story-reading inputs
reader_labels.reason: The text reports substantial representational differences for UniSentEnc relative to ELMO, GoogleLM, and BERT, while BERT is more similar to the LSTM-based models; this supports partial rather than uniform convergence (r1–r5).
